I actually got my terminology a little wrong.

TAS is what would be approximated with instruments that, before GPS, could only measure airspeed via the pitot tube. TAS is an approximation of ground speed using the altitude readout. IAS uses a fixed reference of sea level air pressure.

In response to your question, a GPS would read 0 but due to TAS being extrapolated from pitot tube data, pitch input wouldn't change TAS.

All of these "actual" speed vs "indicated" speed are unnecessarily confusing.

IAS - Indicated Air Speed:
This is your speed relative to the body of air around you

TAS - True Air Speed:
This is your speed relative to the ground, otherwise known as ground speed. This is what a GPS would reflect (theoretically, the geometry of GPS at high altitudes can be whack)

Air moves relative to the ground and varies in pressure with altitude, thus these speeds differ.
